lead.headline: Abu Dhabi will put water investment on the UN agenda for the first time since 2023
lead.dek: The UN Water Conference runs December 8 to 10. It will end with a President's summary, not a negotiated text, so the deals signed around it will matter more than the communiqué.
body: The 2026 United Nations Water Conference, co-hosted by the United Arab Emirates and Senegal, convenes at the Abu Dhabi National Exhibition Centre from December 8 to 10. It is the first UN conference dedicated to water since the 2023 meeting in New York, which was itself the first in nearly half a century. Its stated purpose is to accelerate progress on Sustainable Development Goal 6, clean water and sanitation for all.

Member states adopted six themes for the interactive dialogues in July 2025. One of them, investments for water, is the reason capital providers should be watching. The UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs says the opening day is framed around water for shared prosperity and the closing day around a resilient future built together.

The format sets expectations. IUCN has noted that the conference will produce a summary by the President of the General Assembly instead of a negotiated outcome document. That shifts attention to what gets signed on the margins: sovereign desalination and reuse programs, utility financing frameworks and partnerships with development banks. SIWI has already said World Water Week 2027 will follow up on the commitments made in Abu Dhabi.

pipe.source: Gulf hosts and an African co-chair put scarcity and new supply, desalination above all, at the center of the program.
pipe.treat: PFAS rules in the US and Europe give treatment vendors a regulatory story to bring to sovereign buyers.
pipe.use: Data centers, chip fabs and mining are the industrial demand stories to watch in the side events.
pipe.reuse: Reuse targets are the most bankable commitment a government can make. Watch for numbers, not intentions.
pipe.discharge: Sanitation finance remains the weakest link in SDG 6 and the hardest asset to fund privately.

use.text: Track sovereign desalination and reuse pipelines announced in Abu Dhabi; they become tenders in 2027.
Expect development banks to tie new lending to non-revenue water and reuse targets.
Water risk disclosures for fabs, data centers and mines will draw scrutiny from side events.
Desalination energy, brine and PFAS destruction are the problems buyers will bring.

briefs.headline: US water utilities keep consolidating as American Water and Essential near the finish line
briefs.text: Pennsylvania American Water closed its $32.8 million purchase of the Indian Creek Valley Water Authority system on November 18, adding about 2,600 connections and promising $9 million of upgrades over five years. The larger deal is still moving: Illinois became the fourth state to approve the American Water and Essential Utilities merger, announced November 6, with a Pennsylvania settlement pending approval.
briefs.why: The all-stock merger would create a utility worth about $40 billion serving more than 4.7 million connections, with closing expected in the first quarter of 2027. Small municipal systems remain the steady acquisition pipeline underneath it.

briefs.headline: Veolia adds two Gulf desalination contracts worth nearly €200 million
briefs.text: Veolia won a design contract for the 410,000 cubic meter a day Al Hamriyah plant in Sharjah, which will supply about 1.4 million people, and a five-year contract to operate and optimize the 80,000 cubic meter a day Al Asilah plant in Oman. The French group announced both on November 5.
briefs.why: Operations contracts on existing plants are a growing share of Gulf desalination spending, alongside new build. They give technology owners recurring revenue after construction ends.

briefs.headline: Cox wins the construction contract for Mexico's Rosarito desalination plant
briefs.text: Mexico's National Water Commission awarded the Rosarito construction contract to Cox for about $304 million, after two earlier tenders were declared void. The plant is designed for 2,200 liters a second, about 190,000 cubic meters a day, within a project Conagua has put at $840 million in federal and state investment.
briefs.why: Baja California depends heavily on the Colorado River. A large coastal plant adds a supply source that does not ride on river allocations.

briefs.headline: Utilities still wait on EPA's final PFAS rule
briefs.text: EPA proposed in May to keep the 2024 drinking water limits for PFOA and PFOS while giving qualifying systems two more years, to 2031, to comply, and to rescind limits for four other PFAS. The comment period closed July 20. The agency has said it plans to finalize the changes in 2026.
briefs.why: The compliance date drives treatment capital plans for thousands of systems. Until the final rule lands, utilities are budgeting against two possible deadlines.

company.name: Xylem
company.headline: Xylem is shrinking to grow
company.body: Third quarter results on October 27 missed revenue expectations as utility project timing slipped. Management answered with portfolio moves: it intends to divest Applied Water International and Specialty Flow Control and will report three segments instead of four from 2027. In July it agreed to buy WaterFleet from EagleTree Capital for about $200 million, adding to its industrial water platform.

leader.name: Estelle Brachlianoff
leader.body: Brachlianoff has run Veolia since July 2022, and shareholders renewed her board seat in April 2026 through the 2030 annual meeting. Her GreenUp plan leans on water technology and hazardous waste: Veolia agreed to buy US hazardous waste company Clean Earth for about $3 billion, won two Mumbai water projects in February and launched an integrated offer for data centers.

supplier.name: Ecolab
supplier.headline: Ecolab's water business is being pulled by chips and AI data centers
body: Ecolab reported third quarter sales up 13% to $4.69 billion on October 27, with organic growth accelerating to 7%. Chairman and chief executive Christophe Beck called the quarter an inflection point, and the water segment is where the change shows most clearly.

Global Water sales rose 20% at fixed currency to $2.48 billion. Eleven points came from the Ovivo Electronics and CoolIT acquisitions, and the rest from organic growth led by Global High-Tech, which grew 63% organically on semiconductor and data center demand.

The cost of that bet is visible too. CoolIT amortization and financing took roughly 10% off adjusted earnings growth, holding adjusted EPS to $2.18, up 5%. Management guides full-year adjusted EPS to $8.10 to $8.20.
supplier.why: Fabs and hyperscale data centers now set the pace for industrial water treatment. Expect bundled water, cooling and digital contracts and tighter supply of ultrapure water expertise.

innovation.name: Claros Technologies
innovation.headline: Claros takes PFAS destruction to full scale at Daikin
innovation.body: Most PFAS treatment moves the chemicals into another waste stream. Claros breaks them apart with its ClarosTechUV system. On October 1 it signed a commercial agreement with Daikin America for full-scale deployment at Daikin's plant in Decatur, Alabama, after a December 2025 run treated more than 170,000 gallons of process water with greater than 99.99% destruction of target PFAS.

investor.name: Burnt Island Ventures
investor.headline: The most active water-only venture firm
investor.body: Founded in New York by water industry veteran Tom Ferguson, Burnt Island invests only in early stage water technology. Xylem anchored both of its funds, with climate fund of funds WovenEarth Ventures joining Fund II. Published deal trackers show 2026 investments in Aquatic Labs, Crew Carbon, Biota and Verdi.

capital.intro: Private equity has executed 435 water deals across 25 countries since 2015 and more than doubled its holdings since 2019, according to Bluefield Research. Most of those assets are under three years old, which points to an exit wave.

firm.headline: XPV is buying the unglamorous middle of the water economy

figs.l: Raised for Fund III and Extended Value Fund

firm.body: XPV invests only in water and builds platforms through add-on acquisitions. In 2026 it bought Weisinger, a groundwater and well services provider for Texas municipal and industrial clients, formed the ocean technology platform OceanSight, and added Sound Metrics and C&C Ground Water Services. In June it exited Axius Water alongside co-owner KKR. Founding partner David Henderson leads the firm.

demand.title: Demand keeps climbing as the world adds two billion people
demand.intro: Global water demand has more than doubled since 1960 and has grown by just under 1% a year since the 1980s. The UN expects the population to rise from 8.2 billion in 2024 to a peak of about 10.3 billion in the mid 2080s.

security.headline: The UN says the world has entered water bankruptcy
security.text: A UN University report in January argued that groundwater depletion, overallocation and pollution have pushed many basins past the point of recovery, and that "crisis" no longer describes it.

security.headline: The US and Mexico set Colorado River rules for 2027 and 2028
security.text: The two countries signed a formal agreement in September on new operating guidelines for the river that supplies seven US states and northern Mexico.

security.headline: The Gulf runs on desalination
security.text: The Middle East and North Africa host over 40% of global desalination capacity, and the Gulf Cooperation Council countries alone hold 33%.

place.name: Marina Barrage
place.headline: A dam in the middle of a city that people come to picnic on
body: Marina Barrage closes the 350 meter wide Marina Channel with nine steel crest gates, keeping seawater out and turning the bay into Singapore's 15th reservoir and the first in the city center. Its catchment of about 10,000 hectares is the largest in the country, and the same structure protects low lying downtown streets from flooding.

The pump house is topped by a grass roof of about 11,000 square meters, open around the clock, where people fly kites, picnic and watch the skyline beside a solar installation. National water agency PUB counted close to 15 million visitors in the barrage's first ten years.
place.visit: Free shuttle bus from Marina Bay MRT station. The green roof and public areas are open 24 hours.
place.why: It is the clearest example anywhere of water infrastructure that pays a second dividend: supply, flood control and a public space in one asset.
